3	//! @op SendMessage
4	//! IMPLEMENTED: this operation appends a message to the queue's arrival-order deque in
5	//! [`crate::state`] and answers with its id and content digests. It validates the
6	//! message attributes and the message system attributes the send carries by Amazon SQS's
7	//! documented name, type and value rules, and digests each map into its own
8	//! `MD5Of...` member. On a FIFO queue it
9	//! also honours the FIFO members — it requires a `MessageGroupId`, deduplicates on the
10	//! `MessageDeduplicationId` (supplied, or derived from the body under
11	//! `ContentBasedDeduplication`) and assigns the message a `SequenceNumber`. It is the
12	//! ONLY file to touch for `SendMessage`.
13	//!
14	//! A queue encrypted with a customer managed KMS key is one whose key Amazon SQS has to
15	//! generate a data key under before it can seal the message, as the CALLER — so the
16	//! send is gated on that key being usable and on this caller holding the grant, which is
17	//! [`crate::state::encryption::authorize_queue_key`]; its refusal is answered as the
18	//! `Kms*` error the model declares for each class. The data key itself comes from
19	//! [`crate::state::data_keys`]: the queue's live one while its
20	//! `KmsDataKeyReusePeriodSeconds` window has not run out, else a new one from a
21	//! `kms:GenerateDataKey` call this send makes on the caller's behalf.
22	//!
23	//! ## Shape of an operation

25	//! Each operation is a struct that owns the shared engine and implements
26	//! [`smithy_server_runtime::Operation`]. The framework constructs one per service via
27	//! `SendMessage::new(engine)` and drives it through the centralized request walk:
28	//! deserialize → validate → `handle` → serialize. You write ONLY the `handle` body.

30	//! ## Reaching this service's state

33	//! engine access is guaranteed by the time any request runs. Reach the store through
34	//! [`crate::state::service_state`] and read and write it through the guard it hands back:
35	//!
36	//! ```ignore
37	//!     let state = crate::state::service_state(&*self.engine)
38	//!         .ok_or(/* a modelled server error */)?;
39	//!     state.lock().your_field = /* ... */;

63	//! see the W3C specification for characters. #x9 | #xA | #xD | #x20 to #xD7FF | #xE000 to

66	//! your message body includes only valid characters to avoid this exception.

71	//!   specific message. Valid values: 0 to 900. Maximum: 15 minutes. Messages with a positive
72	//!   DelaySeconds value become available for processing after the delay period is finished.
73	//!   If you don't specify a value, the default value for the queue applies. When you set

83	//!   | #xE000 to #xFFFD | #x10000 to #x10FFFF If a message contains characters outside the

87	//!   (first-in-first-out) queues. The token used for deduplication of sent messages. If a
88	//!   message with a particular MessageDeduplicationId is sent successfully, any messages sent
89	//!   with the same MessageDeduplicationId are accepted successfully but aren't delivered

93	//!   aren't able to provide a MessageDeduplicationId and you enable ContentBasedDeduplication
94	//!   for your queue, Amazon SQS uses a SHA-256 hash to generate the …

96	//!   (First-In-First-Out) and standard queues. In FIFO queues, MessageGroupId organizes
97	//!   messages into distinct groups. Messages within the same message group are always
98	//!   processed one at a time, in strict order, ensuring that no two messages from the same

101	//!   consistent message dwell time across all tenants during noisy neighbor events. Unlike
102	//!   FIFO queues, messages with the same MessageGroupId can be processed in parallel,
103	//!   maintaining the high throughput of standard queues. FIFO …

105	//!   to send. Each message system attribute consists of a Name, Type, and Value. Currently,

111	//!
112	//! ## Output
113	//!
114	//! * `MD5OfMessageAttributes` (String) — An MD5 digest of the non-URL-encoded message
115	//!   attribute string. You can use this attribute to verify that Amazon SQS received the
116	//!   message correctly. Amazon SQS URL-decodes the message before creating the MD5 digest.
117	//!   For information about MD5, see RFC1321.
118	//! * `MD5OfMessageBody` (String) — An MD5 digest of the non-URL-encoded message body string.
119	//!   You can use this attribute to verify that Amazon SQS received the message correctly.
120	//!   Amazon SQS URL-decodes the message before creating the MD5 digest. For information about

122	//! * `MD5OfMessageSystemAttributes` (String) — An MD5 digest of the non-URL-encoded message

124	//!   the message correctly. Amazon SQS URL-decodes the message before creating the MD5

127	//!   queue. For more information, see Queue and Message Identifiers in the Amazon SQS
128	//!   Developer Guide.
129	//! * `SequenceNumber` (String) — This parameter applies only to FIFO (first-in-first-out)
130	//!   queues. The large, non-consecutive number that Amazon SQS assigns to each message. The
131	//!   length of SequenceNumber is 128 bits. SequenceNumber continues to increase for a
132	//!   particular MessageGroupId.

477	        let md5_of_message_attributes = sqs::md5_of_message_attributes(&message_attributes);
478	        // A `Number` attribute carries a number, and the queue holds the number rather
479	        // than the text the request wrote it as; from here on the message is measured and
480	        // stored in that form, so a CONSUMER's digest covers the attributes as delivered.
481	        sqs::store_message_attributes_canonically(&mut message_attributes);

484	        // "All parts of the message attribute, including Name, Type, and Value, are part
485	        // of the message size restriction". A message over it is rejected rather than
486	        // stored. The system attributes are NOT part of it — "the size of a message system
487	        // attribute doesn't count towards the total size of a message" — but they are part
488	        // of what the store retains, so the store's own budget below counts them.
489	        //

491	        // many bytes a message can contain before Amazon SQS rejects it"
492	        // (`SetQueueAttributes$Attributes`), and this is where the request is rejected. The
493	        // NOTIFICATION FAN-OUT of a published message is not such a request: Amazon SNS
494	        // accepted that payload under the TOPIC's own maximum and hands the queue the result,
495	        // so this bound does not bound it and the notification arrives whole
496	        // ([`sqs::service_delivery`]).
497	        let maximum = queue.integer(sqs::MAXIMUM_MESSAGE_SIZE);
498	        let attribute_bytes = sqs::message_attribute_bytes(&message_attributes);
499	        let size = input.message_body.len().saturating_add(attribute_bytes);

501	            && !fanned_out_by_the_notification_service

506	        }

514	        // "If a message with a particular MessageDeduplicationId is sent successfully,

519	        // adds nothing a bound could refuse.

522	            .map(|token| queue.deduplication_key(group_id.as_deref().unwrap_or_default(), token));

525	            .and_then(|key| queue.deduplication.get(key))

527	            return Ok(SendMessageOutput {
528	                md5_of_message_body: Some(md5_of_body),
529	                md5_of_message_attributes,
530	                md5_of_message_system_attributes,
531	                message_id: Some(admitted.message_id.clone()),
532	                sequence_number: Some(admitted.sequence_number.clone()),

534	        }

536	        // What this in-memory store can be made to hold is bounded, counting every byte
537	        // the message retains; a message over the bound is refused rather than accepted
538	        // and silently evicted later.
539	        if let Some(reason) = queue.message_rejection(retained, store_bytes) {

541	                message: Some(reason),

544	        }
545	
546	        let message_id = sqs::new_identifier();
547	        // Only a FIFO queue sequences its messages; `SequenceNumber` "applies only to
548	        // FIFO (first-in-first-out) queues".

552	        // of the send that arrived.
553	        let sender_id = sqs::authorization::sender_id(&*self.engine, ctx);
554	
555	        queue.messages.push_back(sqs::StoredMessage {
556	            message_id: message_id.clone(),
557	            body: input.message_body,
558	            md5_of_body: md5_of_body.clone(),
559	            message_attributes,
560	            message_system_attributes,
561	            message_group_id: group_id,
562	            message_deduplication_id: deduplication_id,
563	            sequence_number: sequence_number.clone(),
564	            sent_at: now,
565	            // The queue this send enqueues the message in is the one it was sent to, so
566	            // its retention runs from the same instant.
567	            retention_from: now,
568	            sender_id,
569	            available_at: sqs::after(now, delay),
570	            invisible_until: None,
571	            receive_count: 0,
572	            queue_receive_count: 0,
573	            first_received_at: None,
574	            last_received_at: None,
575	            // A send puts the message in this queue directly: no redrive moved it here,
576	            // so it names no dead-letter source.
577	            dead_letter_source_arn: None,
578	            // The data key the queue is sealing its messages under, for a queue on a
579	            // customer managed key; a queue on the Amazon SQS owned key needs none.
580	            data_key,
581	        });
582	        if let (Some(key), Some(sequence_number)) = (deduplication_key, sequence_number.clone()) {

584	                key,
585	                sqs::Deduplication {
586	                    message_id: message_id.clone(),
587	                    sequence_number,
588	                    accepted_at: now,
589	                },
590	            );
591	        }
592	        // One message was added to this queue, of the size Amazon SQS measures a message at:

594	        queue.count_sent(size, now);

597	            md5_of_message_body: Some(md5_of_body),

606	/// The KMS refusal of the queue's key, as this operation's own modelled error.

611	/// `KMS.AccessDeniedException`) — carrying the message KMS words that refusal in.

615	        KeyRefusal::NotFound(message) => SendMessageErrorModeled::KmsNotFound(KmsNotFound {

617	        }),
618	        KeyRefusal::Disabled(message) => SendMessageErrorModeled::KmsDisabled(KmsDisabled {

620	        }),
621	        KeyRefusal::InvalidState(message) => {
622	            SendMessageErrorModeled::KmsInvalidState(KmsInvalidState {
623	                message: Some(message),
624	            })
625	        }
626	        KeyRefusal::InvalidKeyUsage(message) => {
627	            SendMessageErrorModeled::KmsInvalidKeyUsage(KmsInvalidKeyUsage {
628	                message: Some(message),
629	            })
630	        }
631	        KeyRefusal::AccessDenied(message) => {
632	            SendMessageErrorModeled::KmsAccessDenied(KmsAccessDenied {
633	                message: Some(message),
634	            })
635	        }
636	    }
637	    .into()
638	}

Problems in `services/service-com-amazonaws-sqs-amazonsqs/src/ops/send_message.rs`. I read only this file, so anything that depends on helpers in `crate::state` is marked as unverified.

**Likely bugs**

1. **KMS work runs before validation and authorization (lines 288-321).** `authorize_queue_key` and `data_key_for_send` run before the queue-policy check (345), the attribute, FIFO and delay validation, the size check and `OverLimit`. Two consequences:
   - A request that is rejected a few lines later can still trigger a `kms:GenerateDataKey` call and refresh the queue's cached data key.
   - A caller the queue policy would deny can see `KmsAccessDenied`, `KmsNotFound` or `KmsDisabled` first. That discloses the queue's key state to someone who may not send to it.
2. **Region and queue lookup are inconsistent (lines 288-294 vs 327-333).** The KMS gate resolves the queue from `input.queue_url` alone, while the actual lookup uses `sqs::request_region`. If the helper resolves by URL across regions, it can judge a different queue than the one that gets written to. I haven't verified this.
3. **Time-of-check to time-of-use gap on the key (lines 288-323).** The key decision and data key are taken before `store.lock()`. The queue can be deleted, recreated or re-keyed in between, and the message is then sealed under a stale `data_key` with no re-check.
4. **Unmodeled states reported as client errors.**
   - A missing service store becomes `UnsupportedOperation` (280-282). That is a server or wiring bug, and it is shown to the client as a 400 for an operation that is supported.
   - If the queue's own `DelaySeconds` is out of range (436-449), the error blames the request with `InvalidParameterValue`. A stored invalid attribute is a bug, not a client mistake.

**Silent defaults and swallowed impossible states**

5. **Empty group id on dedup (line 522).** `group_id.as_deref().unwrap_or_default()` turns an impossible state into `""`. `deduplication_id` is only `Some` on FIFO, and FIFO requires a group id. If that invariant breaks, dedup keys silently collapse across groups. Use `expect` with the invariant, or change the types so it can't happen.
6. **Dedup record can be skipped (line 582).** `if let (Some(key), Some(sequence_number))` skips recording when either is `None`. Both are always `Some` together on FIFO, so a mismatch would silently disable deduplication for that message instead of failing loudly.
7. **Lossy size conversion (line 500).** `i64::try_from(size).unwrap_or(i64::MAX)` substitutes a value on failure. The outcome (rejection) happens to be right, but it should be an explicit `match` or `map_or(true, ...)` so the intent is visible.
8. **Canonicalization can't fail (line 481).** `store_message_attributes_canonically(&mut ...)` returns `()`. If a `Number` can fail to parse there, the failure is swallowed. Check that `message_attribute_refusal` fully guarantees parseability.

**Error ordering and coverage**

9. **Body validation precedes queue lookup (lines 260-278).** A send to a nonexistent queue with an empty or invalid body returns `MissingParameter` or `InvalidMessageContents` instead of `QueueDoesNotExist`. This is unauthenticated-style validation ahead of resource and permission checks.
10. **`kms_refusal` can't produce two modeled errors (lines 612-638).** `KmsOptInRequired` and `KmsThrottled` are declared in the enum but `KeyRefusal` has no variants for them, so they are unreachable. The same goes for `RequestThrottled`, `InvalidAddress` and `InvalidSecurity`. If any of these is intentionally unsupported, say so; otherwise it is a coverage gap.
11. **Dedup resend returns the new request's digests (lines 527-533).** The resend answers with `md5_of_body`, `md5_of_message_attributes` and `md5_of_message_system_attributes` of the new request, but the original `message_id` and `sequence_number`. If the resend differs from the original, the digests no longer describe the message that was admitted.

**Lower severity**

12. **Calls made under the state lock.** `authorization::denied` and `authorization::sender_id` (345, 553) run while `store.lock()` is held. This contradicts the comment at 296-310, which says external calls happen before the lock. It is a deadlock risk if those helpers touch engine state that the SQS lock also guards.
13. **Mixed error construction.** Errors come from `Scaffolded::invalid_parameter_value(...)` with `String` and `&'static str`, from `sqs::*_message` helpers, and from hand-built `format!` strings (444, 458). The messages' wording and the code that builds them are scattered, so they will drift.
14. **Needless clones on the error path.** `input.message_attributes.clone()` and `input.message_system_attributes.clone()` (359-362, 451-454) copy the full maps even when the request is about to be refused.
